speaker: EN_A
text: So the latest SIA data for March just came out and it looks like semiconductor shipments are picking up. Is this the recovery everyone has been waiting for?

speaker: EN_B
text: It definitely looks encouraging. Shipments for integrated circuits excluding memory were up 29 percent month over month in March. That is well above the typical seasonal pattern.

speaker: EN_A
text: 29 percent is a big number. But is this broad based or just driven by a few segments?

speaker: EN_B
text: Actually it was pretty broad based. Most sub-segments shipped above seasonal levels. Analog and microcontrollers both showed strong momentum. But there are two notable exceptions.

speaker: EN_A
text: Let me guess. DRAM and something else?

speaker: EN_B
text: Exactly. DRAM shipments only grew 5 percent month over month, which is below the historical average of 9 percent. So memory is starting to moderate. Meanwhile NAND was the standout with 34 percent growth, way above normal.

speaker: EN_A
text: So DRAM is cooling down. Does that mean the memory super cycle is ending?

speaker: EN_B
text: That is the big question. The report flags that DRAM is clearly decelerating but it does not fully answer whether this is a temporary pause or a structural shift. That is one of the things the full report explores in more detail.

speaker: EN_A
text: And where does the industry stand relative to long term demand?

speaker: EN_B
text: On a three month moving average basis, IC units excluding memory are now only 4 percent below the long term trend line. In February that gap was 8 percent. So we are seeing steady but measured improvement.

speaker: EN_A
text: Steady but not explosive. That matches what a lot of companies have been saying in earnings calls.

speaker: EN_B
text: Exactly. Companies are saying they are shipping closer to end demand but the pace of improvement is gradual. The data confirms that narrative.

speaker: EN_A
text: Which segment is still the furthest from normal?

speaker: EN_B
text: Microcontrollers. They are still 26 percent below trend. That is a huge gap. Analog on the other hand is only 2 percent below trend, almost back to normal.

speaker: EN_A
text: So MCU is where the biggest recovery opportunity lies?

speaker: EN_B
text: That is what the report suggests. It says they prefer names that are shipping furthest below trend with differentiated supply chain management. But the report does not fully unpack why MCU is recovering so slowly. That is another question the full version digs into.

speaker: EN_A
text: So the big picture is a moderate recovery with clear winners and laggards.

speaker: EN_B
text: Correct. Analog and NAND are close to normal. MCU and DRAM still have work to do. The full report goes deeper into specific stock implications and risk factors.

speaker: EN_A
text: Where can our listeners find that full analysis?

speaker: EN_B
text: Check the show notes. We share full report breakdowns in our community. Thanks for listening and we will catch you next time.
